messages.body_plain:
Dear geomorph group,

I'm currently working on a project looking at species delimitation among morphologically similar pairs of endangered land snail species, utilizing historical museum collections to identify potential shifts in morphology or loss of morphological diversity that explain current trends and apparent convergence of morphology.

I have PCA plots for both contemporary populations and historical populations, with convex hulls on them to show overlap and morphological limits for the species. I'm trying to work out basically what the morphospace extent of each species (as the total area of the convex hull for each species), the overlap in convex hulls between the pairs of species, and the proportion of that overlap in relation to the entire species morphospace, with values for both historical and contemporary populations.

I've been looking through the vignette and have not been able to find anything, but does anyone know of a way to be able to calculate these values within the package? I've done morphological disparity work to look at diversity, alongside discriminant analysis and statistical delimitation, but this would be a really cool way to visually explain and explore what is happening.

Thanks in advance for your help!

Chris

messages.body_plain:
Chris,

You might want to check out the package, geometry, It has a vignette for the convhulln function, which can calculate hull areas/volumes.

In terms of overlap, although maybe a little inelegant, one can calculate the area of two hulls (in two dimensions), plus one hull that combines the points of the two hulls.  If there is little or no overlap, the one hull will have a much larger area than either of the two hulls, individually.  If there is considerable overlap, the area of the one hull will resemble the areas of the two hulls.  A good way to evaluate this is compare AC, the area of the third hull comprising points of both groups to AA + AB, the sum of the areas of the hulls of individual groups; i.e., AC / (AA +AB).  This value will start to exceed 1 if the hulls do not overlap, or do not overlap much, but will be considerably less than 1 if they overlap substantially.

I have to also warn against conclusions made in two-dimension projections.  Imagine two discoidal clouds of points with no overlap at all in a third PC dimension, viewed from a two-dimensional projection of PC1 and PC2.  One might conclude that the groups share the same space, when they don’t.  Luckily, convhulln can handle volumes of hulls in n dimensions.

Hope that helps,
Mike

Dear Ian, Mike, Dean and Antigoni,

thank you for great advices! Percentile confidence intervals for my data were indeed very asymmetric. Thanks to your help, I was able to compute BCa confidence intervals using boot package. Below is the solution for the plethodon dataset in case if someone wanders into this thread.

Thank you for answering my question!
Kind regards,
Marina

library(geomorph)
library(boot)
library(broom)

data(plethodon)
Y.gpa <- gpagen(plethodon$land)
gdf <- geomorph.data.frame(Y.gpa,
                           site = plethodon$site,
                           species = plethodon$species)

fit_full <- procD.lm(coords ~ log(Csize) + site * species, data = gdf,
                     iter = 999, print.progress = FALSE)
gp <- interaction(plethodon$site, plethodon$species)

# disparity
md <- tapply(rowSums(resid(fit_full)^2), gp, mean)

# function to compute md on bootstrapped data
get_md <- function(data, indices, fit, gp){
  Z <- data[indices, ]

  form <-fit$LM$form
  gdf2 <- fit$LM$data

  gdf2$Y <- Z[, -1]
  gdf2$Csize <- Z[, 1] # non universal (need to change the variable name
                       # to match the name in the data and formula)
  New_fit_full <- procD.lm(form, data = gdf2, iter = 0, print.progress = FALSE)

  d2.i <- rowSums(resid(New_fit_full)^2)
  smr <- by(d2.i, gp, mean)
  smr
}

# bootstrap
set.seed(302354)
boot_out <- boot(data = cbind(gdf$Csize, fit_full$LM$Y),
                 statistic = get_md,
                 R = 1000, # increase for final calculation
                 strata = gp, # bootstrap by group
                 fit = fit_full,
                 gp = gp)
# tidy confidence limits with BCa for all groups via broom package
tidy_cl <- tidy(boot_out, conf.int <http://conf.int> = TRUE, conf.method = "bca")

library(ggplot2)
ggplot(data = tidy_cl, aes(x = term, y = statistic)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high))

> Marina et al. (Mike, Dean and Antigoni),
>
> To add to both Mike and Dean's point on using (non-parametric) bootstrapping based on empirical resampling to compute confidence intervals.
>
> As mentioned in a couple of the papers/books that Dean mentioned, the "percentile"  based confidence intervals (like Mike calculated) are usually an ok starting point,  but are often problematic for somewhat skewed distributions (of resampled estimates, not raw data),  when the observed estimate is near a boundary (e.g. the observed value is close to the minimum possible value it can take for the data set) and with small within group sample sizes. There are some immediate checks (the boot library can help) and the Bias Corrected and Accelerated CIs (BCa) often can provide an improvement. These problems do occur more often for "variance"/"disparity" and phenotypic integration related statistics in my experience (which makes sense because of both being higher moment statistics that are estimated and also are used bounded by a minimum value, with real estimates sometimes "near" that value).  Like Mike showed in the first example, it is usually most sensible to do the sampling within groups of focus (in the boot library this is done via the strata argument, but it is relatively straightforward to code like Mike showed).
>
> So it pays to take some time and patience to work on this. For the particular data set that Mike showed the example for, things mostly behaved reasonably well. In other situations (see our methods in Haber and Dworkin 2017 in Evolution for some discussion of these issues), things can get a bit bonkers though!
>
> The most robust approach for generating CIs from non parametric bootstrapping (sampling with replacement) is the studentized bootstrap. This has greater computational demands as it requires bootstraps of bootstrap samples (to generate standard errors of each resampled data set to normalize the value we use each iteration). Typically (in my experience) this requires about 200 iterations in the internal resampling, so for a typical "10000" bootstrap iterations, it is really computationally more like 20,000,000 iterations total. Thankfully there are ways of making this more efficient so it still (on a relatively new laptop) will only be on the order of 10-20 minutes to run all these iterations. It can also be parallelized relatively easily in R (with some package dependencies). I keep meaning to write a little add-on set of functions to interact with geomorph/RRPP model objects to do so (I have some working examples just with base R, lm functions not with geomorph). But, alas no time until at least the end of next semester. But if someone does bug me I will work on it. I keep meaning to, but I keep thinking it is just us who suffers with this.

messages.body_plain:
Marina,

I’m happy you were able to solve this.  It looks like your results are superficially similar to the within-group results I previously found, despite different confidence limits summarized.  It should not be a surprise that confidence intervals are asymmetric if the statistic is a variance, which must be positive.  Any “odd” outcomes (e.g., frequent sampling of values that produce large residuals) will be extreme in a positive direction, which will positively skew the distribution of random variances.  I’m willing to bet a log-transformation of the variances will produce symmetric confidence intervals.

Best,
Mike

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I am having some issues to understand what's going on with the shapes on the min and max of the PC axes when I am using the residuals instead of the raw data.

For the background: I landmarked caecilians skulls and I want to check for relationships between burrowing force and neurocranium shape. I performed my GPA and I got the Y.gpa$coords. I can then perform a PCA ( T1 <- gm.prcomp(Y.gpa$coords)), and try to warp my ref mesh towards the min and max of the PC1 for example. Although I don't manage to do that using the 'warpRefMesh' function, I did it with 'tps3d' and 'shade3d' functions (Grey picture). So far, so good.

However, I would like to display the same max and min warped meshes using the residuals with the log(Csize). So I used 'procD.lm' function to get these residuals:

plethAnova <- procD.lm(Y.gpa$coords~logCsize, iter = 999, RRPP=TRUE)
shape.resid <- arrayspecs(plethAnova$residuals,p=dim(Y.gpa$coords)[1], k=dim(Y.gpa$coords)[2])
adj.shape <- shape.resid + array(Y.gpa$coords, dim(shape.resid))

And I think, that here, adj.shape are my shape coordinates corrected for size as I wanted. However, if I run again a PCA on adj.shape, and I warp the ref mesh towards max-min on a PC, I have extremely weird shapes (Green picture).

If I extract the residuals with LogCsize using another function, the Common Allometric Component function, and that I display again max and min shapes, results are totally different, but way less weird (Blue picture).

At this point, I don't know anymore what to use to get my corrected shape variation data, and why I have so different results between the two different functions. Is there any chance I did something wrong to get the adj.shape data that could explain why I have so 'weird' shapes ? I am not saying the green one isn't correct, maybe the shape variation on this PC is located on the snout and the quadrate-squamosal complex, which would explains the weird shape. But as I have big differences between the two functions, I might have done something wrong somewhere...

Thanks a lot!

Best,

Aurélien

Below is a step to do that easily with your code.

Best,
Mike

plethAnova  <- procD.lm(Y.gpa$coords~logCsize, iter = 999, RRPP=TRUE)

plethNULL <- procD.lm(Y.gpa$coords~ 1, iter = 999, RRPP=TRUE)

shape.resid <- arrayspecs(plethAnova$residuals, p=dim(Y.gpa$coords)[1], k=dim(Y.gpa$coords)[2])
shape.mean <- arrayspecs(plethNULL$fitted, p=dim(Y.gpa$coords)[1], k=dim(Y.gpa$coords)[2])

adj.shape <- shape.mean + shape.resid

Raol,

This cannot be implemented in geomorph. Also, I would not recommend the procedure for evaluating trends in multivariate data. The procedure is basically one that forces multivariate data to a number line, and then performs statistics on those values. Such methods are well-known to identify patterns that don’t exist, or not find patterns that do exist.

Essentially, the values ‘d’ are one-dimensional projections in a space described by the independent variables, not the actual data. Then, this is used in the ancova. But differences among groups are not guaranteed to align with the first PC axis of the H-matrix: which is how ‘d’ is derived.

This convoluted algebra (forcing multivariate data to a single dimension for further analysis) is also unnecessary. Divergence between groups (which is what the divergence vector ‘d’ attempts to describe), may be estimated directly in the full multivariate space. The function pairwise does this for example. Then, one may statistically compare these using RRPP and associated Z-scores.

messages.body_plain:
Raul,

You can get SSCPs using RRPP::manova.update on a procD.lm object.  You can perform eigen-analysis on these vectors, and data projections might give you some useful visual tools for visualizing, e.g., shape change associated with an effect.

I must warn you though against following the methods of that paper from that point on.  If you use the projected scores as data in other analyses, as that paper does, you introduce not only a circular line of reasoning into your data analysis, but strictly a bias, that renders the results unworthy of trust.

The divergence scores — data projected onto d — are scores that maximize a difference between treatments, irrespective of noise or other effects, that if used univariately are sure to find a treatment difference, because that is what you set out to do by calculating d.  This makes absolutely no sense.  Think about it, one is aligning a vector that best characterizes differences between groups and then asking if those groups are different, only along the vector where they were made to be most different.

The reason you cannot do this directly in geomorph is because it is asinine to do.  You can acquire the parts but your own assembly is required.

Best,
Mike

I am trying remove the effects of specimen bending in my landmarks by removing the PC that describes the bending, and then backtransforming to get adjusted coordinates, as in these papers: https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1558-5646.2007.00259.x,  https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1558-5646.2012.01622.x. My question is how do I get V from the gm.prcomp output, if this is possible? I initially expected from the documentation that V would be the $rotation matrix, but it has a different number of columns from $x, so Z and V are non-conformable and can't be multiplied.

For reference, my landmark array is [24 x 2 x 51], $x is [51 x 46], and $rotation is [48 x 48], and the line I am trying to use to execute the above formula is: pca$x%*%t(pca$rotation)+rowMeans(pca$rotation).

thanks very much in advance,
Grant

Grant,

You have one of two choices.  You can append columns of 0s to V and Z to make it have the same number of columns as X, or better, set tol = 0 as an argument in gm.prcomp.  (Note, gm.prcomp uses RRPP::ordinate to perform ordinations.  The arguments from the ordinate function can, therefore, be adjusted.  See the help file for ordinate to understand more about adjusting dimensions.)

The defaults for gm.prcomp (and ordinate) shave off redundant dimensions, which is a result of size, orientation, position, and possibly autocorrelation of semilandmarks in GPA producing a data space that has fewer dimensions than one might expect based on the number of Cartesian coordinates.  In order to make the math work, you need to retain these redundant dimensions.  Setting tol = 0 will allow that.

Hope that helps.  Good luck!

Mike

messages.subject: Allometry-corrected shape analysis
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I am hoping for some clarification/help on doing allometry-corrected shape analysis. I am analysing the beak shapes of 2 lines of chickens. I have run the following code in Geomorph and get significant P-values suggesting that there is an allometric effect.

gdf <- geomorph.data.frame(gpa_ppdata, line = pcadata$line)

#Does shape correlate with size (single multivariate regression)?
fit.size <- procD.lm(coords ~ log(Csize), data = gdf, iter = 999, RRPP = FALSE, print.progress = FALSE)
anova(fit.size)

#Does shape differ between lines (single factor MANOVA)?
fit.line <- procD.lm(coords ~ line, data = gdf, iter = 999, RRPP = FALSE, print.progress = FALSE)
anova(fit.line)

#Does shape differ between lines, while accounting for shape covarying with size (single factor MANCOVA)?
fit.size.line <- procD.lm(coords ~ log(Csize) * line, data = gdf, iter = 999, RRPP = FALSE, print.progress = FALSE)
anova(fit.size.line)

Now I would like to correct for allometry and use the residuals to generate another PCA plot and run the ANOVAs again but I am just not sure which residuals to use (fit.size, fit.line, or fit.size.line).

For comparing residuals, is the code the same as above? For example,

resid1 <- fit.size$residuals
gdf2 <- geomorph.data.frame(gpa_ppdata, line = pcadata$line, PC1 = pcadata$Comp1, resid1 = resid1)
fit.size.allom <- procD.lm(resid1 ~ log(Csize), data = gdf2, iter = 999, RRPP = FALSE, print.progress = FALSE)

I have read through previous threads about removing the allometric effect but I'm not confident on which code best fits my data. Any help would be very much appreciated!

Thank you,

Sarah

messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] Allometry-corrected shape analysis
messages.body_plain:
Sarah,

Based on your code, the object fit.size$residuals are in fact the allometry-free residual shape components. However, be aware that if your ancova model fit.size.line displays a significant interaction term with a large effect size (Z-score), this indicates that the allometry patterns differ among groups. In that case, using fit.size$residuals as allometry-free shape is inappropriate, as those residuals are based on a common slope model.

And in that case, the residuals from the full model fit.size.line aren’t useful for downstream investigation, as they are not comparable among groups (different allometry lines are fit to each group, so residuals are not from the same thing).

Finally, it makes little sense to do the last model you have: procD.lm(resid1 ~ log(Csize).   The residuals already have the effect of log(Csize) removed so this will likely not glean any additional insight.

Dean

> Based on your code, the object fit.size$residuals are in fact the allometry-free residual shape components. However, be aware that if your ancova model fit.size.line displays a significant interaction term with a large effect size (Z-score), this indicates that the allometry patterns differ among groups. In that case, using fit.size$residuals as allometry-free shape is inappropriate, as those residuals are based on a common slope model.
>
>
>
> And in that case, the residuals from the full model fit.size.line aren’t useful for downstream investigation, as they are not comparable among groups (different allometry lines are fit to each group, so residuals are not from the same thing).
>
>
>
> Finally, it makes little sense to do the last model you have: procD.lm(resid1 ~ log(Csize).   The residuals already have the effect of log(Csize) removed so this will likely not glean any additional insight.
>
>

>
>
>
> #Does shape correlate with size (single multivariate regression)?

>
> anova(fit.size)
>
